questions.explain: Synchronous commit waits for hardening — the secondary has the log durably on disk — not for redo, which is the separate stage of replaying log into data files.
options: The secondary to redo the log into its data files, so reads see the change
The secondary to harden the log blocks to its own log disk
The secondary to replay all queued redo and return an empty send queue
The secondary to acknowledge the listener DNS TTL before commit
questions.q: In an Availability Group with synchronous commit, what exactly does the primary wait for before acknowledging the commit to the client?

questions.explain: The transaction log on the primary cannot be truncated past the oldest log needed by any secondary. A dead secondary shows log_reuse_wait_desc = AVAILABILITY_REPLICA — an unmonitored stall is a disk-full incident waiting to happen.
options: The secondary is applying log faster than the primary can send, causing backpressure
The primary is committing too slowly because synchronous hardening is enabled
The distribution database is full and blocking the Log Reader Agent
A disconnected secondary is preventing log truncation on the primary — the log will keep growing
questions.q: You see log_reuse_wait_desc = 'AVAILABILITY_REPLICA' on the primary and the transaction log keeps growing. What is happening?

questions.explain: AGs do not cascade — a secondary cannot forward log blocks. For fan-out across sites, use a distributed availability group: a forwarder secondary on the remote site feeds the remote AG's primary, which fans out locally.
options: A distributed availability group, where a remote forwarder feeds the remote AG's primary
A chain of cascading AG secondaries, each forwarding log blocks downstream
Transactional replication from each secondary to the next secondary
Linked servers daisy-chained with OPENQUERY log shipping
questions.q: AGs do not cascade secondaries. How does the chapter recommend building a fan-out topology across multiple sites?

questions.explain: sp_posttracertoken posts a tracer token to a publication and sp_helptracertokenhistory reads how long the token took through each agent — the chapter's method for measuring end-to-end transactional replication latency.
options: DBCC CHECKDB with the PHYSICAL_ONLY option, timed against the distribution database
Querying sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states for log_send_rate
Posting a tracer token with sp_posttracertoken and reading it back with sp_helptracertokenhistory
Running sys.fn_cdc_map_time_to_lsn between publisher and subscriber
questions.q: How do you measure true end-to-end latency of SQL Server transactional replication?

questions.explain: After a forced failover the old primary's log chain has diverged, so it cannot simply rejoin as a secondary — it must be re-seeded via automatic seeding or backup/restore before rejoining the AG.
options: Automatic failover immediately replays the old primary's log and promotes it back
The old primary must be re-seeded before rejoining, because its log chain diverged
The old primary can rejoin as a readable secondary with no action required
The old primary's log is truncated and it becomes the new distribution database
questions.q: After a forced failover with data loss, what must happen before the old primary can rejoin the Availability Group?
